subLevels.german: Es gibt vier Jahreszeiten: Frühling, Sommer, Herbst und Winter.
subLevels.reveal: Zeit = "time" (as in our borrowed word "zeitgeist"), so Jahreszeit = "time of year". Herbst ~ "harvest", as you may have guessed! Frühling has no cognate in English; it roughly means "the early one", and it's the same "-ling" as in "duckling".

subLevels.german: Ich habe eine Frühlingsrolle zum Frühstück gegessen.

hints.hint: We saw gegessen in Jemand hat von meinem Brei gegessen, a complaint all of the Bären could have made. The auxiliary + verb here can be translated as "I have verb-ed", or "I verb-ed".
Frühling means "the early one", so Frühstück is an early meal.

subLevels.reveal: Nice one! This is not, admittedly, a typical German Frühstück — bread and cheese, cold cuts and eggs are more agreeable to the German palate.

subLevels.instruction: Match the weather words (−1 pt per wrong placement)
subLevels.reveal: -ig ~ "-y" and -isch is just "-ish", so Germans literally say it's "rain-ish"!

hints.hint: Think a common form of precipitation seen im Winter.

subLevels.reveal: Es in Es gibt ("there is/are") and Es in Es schneit ("it snows") are the same dummy "it" — doesn't refer to anything specific, just filling in as a placeholder to keep the grammar happy. English uses "there" for existence and "it" elsewhere, but German economically uses es for both.

hints.hint: Schnee is the noun form of the verb we just saw.

subLevels.reveal: gleich and "(a)like" are direct cognates! The g- came from a prefix that English dropped (but retained in some words as a fossilized a-, as in "alike").

subLevels.german: Meine Katze mag sonniges Wetter — sie schläft den ganzen Tag in der Sonne.

hints.hint: We last saw the verb schläft with a separable prefix with Goldlöckchen schläft in Bärchens Bett ein.

subLevels.reveal: sie is actually the feminine pronoun "she", but this particular Katze happens to be a boy, and that's okay! It's purely because Katze is a feminine noun, so the pronoun follows suit. Grammatical gender doesn't have to match the sex of the referent. The most famous example: das Mädchen ("the girl, maiden") is actually a third category called neuter, not feminine!
subLevels.revealImageAlt: A very cute orange tabby cat with a blue leash sleeping on a step in the sun.

subLevels.german: Sommerkleidung ist leicht, Winterkleidung ist warm.

hints.hint: Kleid ~ "clad". What can you be clad in?

subLevels.reveal: Kleidung has not one but two cognates in English — "clothing" and "cladding" (clothing for buildings!). We also retain the verb form "clad" as in "clad in shining armour", but it does sound a little medieval.

subLevels.german: Es regnet und regnet und regnet. Das Wetter ist so schlecht!

hints.hint: regnet is the verb form of Regen — rain.
schlecht is the opposite of gut — as in Guten Tag!

subLevels.reveal: This sentence is likely to be applicable between 1/3 and 1/2 of the time in Germany. But of course Germans don't take that lying down!

subLevels.german: Es gibt kein schlechtes Wetter, nur schlechte Kleidung.
subLevels.reveal: This saying is probably not German in origin, but it's a sentiment that Germans have definitely embraced.

subLevels.german: Du bist doch nicht aus Zucker!
subLevels.explanation: doch is a famously untranslatable emphatic particle, and can be rendered in many ways — here its emphasis is represented by "C'mon".

hints.hint: This exhortation follows naturally from Es gibt kein schlechtes Wetter, nur schlechte Kleidung.
Zucker has a direct cognate in English, and both words were borrowed ultimately from Arabic "sukkar".

subLevels.reveal: And that's the whole German philosophy of weather: stop complaining, grab your Regenmantel, and get outside. Take a break and I'll see you in the next level!
